We wanted to be one of the first ones to open up, we wanted to do the rollout as quick as possible. Since April, since I got licensed, I have not stopped — with vendors, companies, landlords — and I'm only opening January 4th. Everybody I go to is either charging way too much for rent, or the area isn't where I want to be. Most of these landlords are truthfully just scumbags — I give them what they want and they still want everything else. A few landlords, I accepted all their terms — six-month deposit, $20,000 a month — and they still come back wanting equity too, and then denied me when I said no. That's not what I'm used to. My first business, Ruth's Bag — my brother, Rob, is my partner here, my partner at the dry cleaners, and was my partner in that business too. We've been opening up businesses together as long as I can remember, my first one at 18 years old. I've never gone through this ever, opening retail, opening offices — never gone through this. It's like all these landlords are working together in a way, because it happened with every single one, until I met the Zar family, who owned this property. They were humble, amazing guys — that's the only reason I'm mentioning their name. They didn't take advantage of me, they were very welcoming, the space was beautiful, and that's why we settled in this area.

Bryan Fields: So you guys settled on a location on the Upper East Side, a higher-end part of the city, a month before the injunction. Was this all part of your business plan, or was it thrown out the window from all these obstacles, and now you're flying by the seat of your pants?

Markel Bababekov: So we made a business plan, 78 pages, day one — once we got licensed, my brother and I made a legit business plan immediately, and we followed it for a long time. But I realized very quickly the cannabis business doesn't work like that. I ripped that shit up, threw it in the garbage.

Bryan Fields: Did you build the predatory cannabis tax into your business plan? Like, here's a line item, additional 25%, whatever?

Markel Bababekov: I should have — then I would have known my budget needed to be a couple hundred grand more just because of that. It's been such a shit show in New York, and I'm loving it though, don't get me wrong. I'm finally, for the first time, doing something I love so much, something I'm so passionate about, I enjoy it. So even though it's been a shit show, I've been riding the shit show with a smile.

Bryan Fields: That's the space, right, and I think the important part is that the cannabis industry has this allure for a lot of people, but once you get into it, you recognize it operates differently.

Markel Bababekov: One of the hardest industries to be in. Listen, I own a dry cleaning factory, so I purchase materials people can do harmful things with, solvents, and in this industry you have to track this material every time you buy it. I thought that was hard, with the inspections. Coming into this space, it's ten times harder than I ever imagined with the regulations. I replaced my window signs three times because of the regulations — they keep giving us new ones constantly. I'm like $18,000 in a hole just for window signs right now. It's a hard space to get into, guys, a very hard space. If you want to be in the cannabis space, you need so much patience, so much time, a really good team behind you — media team, marketing team, PR team — and truthfully, it's all going to be worth it.

Bryan Fields: I want to stay on the story — you finally lock in the location, you're probably ecstatic, you can lock in some of those line items on the business plan that needs to be refreshed, and then the injunction happens a month later. What was the internal process like? What were you doing in that moment?

Markel Bababekov: A month before the injunction happened, I signed a heavy lease — like a $2 million lease — on the Upper East Side, and a month later we find out about the injunction. OCM texted me. I was in LA, still going back and forth — I permanently moved back to New York in September. I was in LAX, just got off the shuttle bus to get into the airport, coming to New York, and OCM calls me, saying, 'Hey, we need one last thing from you for licensing.' I said, 'Yeah, I'll get it to you tomorrow.' The next day I find out about the injunction, and everything shut down — the whole city's cannabis industry shut down overnight. I called my lawyers, my whole team, and asked, 'What do we do? Can we still continue, should we continue?' We had just gotten the space, already started the buildout two weeks prior, already paid vendors a lot of deposits to start the buildout. We decided to probably make a very dumb business move which really paid off — we never stopped anything, it was business as usual, we continued the buildout. OCM couldn't talk with us, they weren't allowed to, so I couldn't get my license from them, couldn't get any emails, nothing. I was going in blind, off the regulations and my lawyers' information, and we just did it — paying all these people, spending hundreds of thousands of dollars without knowing what was going to happen, which was the scariest part. I sold one of my dry cleaners in LA to invest in this business, moved my kids to New York for this. When all this happened, I felt like I was Willy Wonka in the Chocolate Factory and I just got the golden ticket and it was getting taken away and I'd never get it back — that's how I felt. But we never stopped, we kept the buildout going. We were in the courthouses all the time, supporting the cannabis market in New York. It was one bad thing after the other, the judge constantly going against OCM. It was such a shit show, so my brother and I were starting to think we should pull the plug now before we had everything invested. I'm so glad we didn't, because about two weeks later I found out I made the short list, one of the few shops that could open during the injunction, thank God. We then put the acceleration on everything, telling everybody, 'We need this by this day.' Thankfully everything came together. But the injunction, man, it was so many emotions, high and low — thinking I'm going to do this in a few weeks, all the way down to, 'What the hell did I just do, selling this business, moving across the country, and this whole thing's about to blow up in my face.'

Bryan Fields: I want to go back to you and your brother having that conversation about maybe pulling the plug — what were some of the scenarios, could you get out of the lease?

Markel Bababekov: We called our landlord, told them the situation — 'Not our fault, we signed with you a month later and the court put a stop on everything.' I told them this is pretty much as close as you can get to a national emergency for the weed industry in New York — like we just got COVID in the New York cannabis space, that's what it felt like to me. I said we need a way out of the lease if the shit hits the fan and we don't get our license. Luckily we were able to get out — it said in the lease that if we do not get our final license we can back out, but the problem is they keep our deposit, and the deposit is well over six figures, a lot of money. So I was thinking, okay, I'm going to lose almost a quarter million in a deposit if I stop this right now, and another couple hundred grand to designers, media, millwork contractors, because I gave a bunch of people deposits that month. So we're going to lose at least $400,000 out the door no matter what, but if we just keep going and put in another couple hundred, we finish it. We would have lost more pulling the plug, truthfully. We were so heavily invested at that point it made no sense to stop, but it also made no sense to stop in case the injunction got lifted tomorrow and we needed to open. My brother and I weighed everything, put all the numbers together, and made a logical conclusion that we'd already put way too much sweat equity into this, and if we pulled out now we'd regret it 100%.

Bryan Fields: I give you a ton of credit, because I think that's a really hard decision — you were pot committed financially and going to proceed through the long haul without knowing how long the injunction process would take. The hard part is you're waiting on updates, praying these things get resolved, and you're not the only one experiencing this.

Markel Bababekov: Real quick — I'm part of the CAURD Coalition, which I think rebranded as the New York Cannabis Retail Association or something. All the CAURD licensees are in a Discord app, and everybody was going through emotions for three, four months straight — 'Hey, I need a vendor for this, my grand opening is going to be this' — everybody just venting about everything to do with cannabis in New York in that Discord. Everybody thought they were about to lose everything, and all these emotions were flying in one space. There was so much negative energy throughout the injunction, nobody wanted to do anything until they knew what was going on, and we were getting negative energy from other owners because we communicate a lot. A few people even told us, 'Why are you still putting money into it, you're not allowed to open, it makes no sense.'

Bryan Fields: And at the same time, the illicit market is thriving — here you are in complete holdup trying to do everything right, with all this money sunk in, and they're just thriving. Take us through your position right now — do you have illegal dispensaries around you?

Markel Bababekov: Yes. There are a few illicit shops next to me — unfortunately one right across the street, and another a couple blocks down. You'll know very quickly what an illicit shop looks like versus mine. The illicit shops are heavy on green marketing, weed leaves everywhere, promoting 'we sell weed.' We don't do that, because of kids — we don't want ten, eleven, twelve-year-olds seeing that abrupt marketing. We don't want the community getting mad at us either. When you go inside a smoke shop, it's just another hole in the wall, product piled on top of each other, hundreds of SKUs, ugly, messy. The guy next door has a couple jars, maybe six flavors of flower, three or four flavors of vapes — one of the vape brands he carries actually came to us too, a licensed company from LA, and we denied them because they're selling to illicit shops. If you're a vendor selling to illicit shops, there's no room in our store for you.

Bryan Fields: So just to clarify for our listeners — the shop that looks like a weed shop based on promotion is actually the illegal one, and the shop that's discreet and doesn't look like a weed shop is the legal one?

Markel Bababekov: Exactly that, yes. Regulations, again — from outside, on the smoke shop you can look in and see all the weed products. In our store you will not see any products from outside because we don't want kids or people who don't want to see it to be able to. Everything is blacked out. We do it for a reason and we're okay with it. And this guy next to me, none of his products are lab tested, his flower isn't prepackaged, who knows where he's getting it from, who knows about pesticides — there's so much that can go wrong if you don't test every product. I wouldn't even touch it. There's a very big difference — my store is elegant, not everything piled on top of each other, your eyes don't wander everywhere, we've got some of the best products in New York, I tried every single product myself to make sure it's good enough for my shelves, and a few brands we had to turn down. These smoke shops, I know they're my competition, but they're not really my competition — they have maybe ten or twelve SKUs, this specific smoke shop, and I have over 300 SKUs of some of the best product in New York. But still, we've got to get them closed, or at least get them to stop selling without a license.

Bryan Fields: Was it always the plan to be discreet and community-oriented rather than built out for tourism?

Markel Bababekov: No, it was not. When we were first closing on stores, there were three or four stores in Times Square that we wanted to close on, wanting to be a tourist destination — back in April of last year. But keep in mind, the information given to us by OCM wasn't accurate either — we were told we'd get funding, a loan with low interest, and stores built out for us. So I was trying to get the best store in the best area thinking that's what was going to happen, then quickly found out that's not a fact at all. Santa's not real, and DASNY is a bigger shit show than the city — but I still have to give credit to the city, they're still doing a great job, I love everybody at OCM, but DASNY, terrible at what they're doing. So my brother and I had that talk — are we doing it through the DASNY fund, self-funded, or going big and getting shareholders? We found out what DASNY's terms were like, the buyout options, terrible stuff, no businessman should sign anything like that, so we crossed that out. We didn't want to be one of those companies with a bunch of people behind us where our voice doesn't count, so we crossed that out too, and decided to do it just between me and my brother. Then we had to rethink where we were going to open, because Times Square was no longer an option for a small family-owned business. We're on the Upper East Side, been here ten years, know the community, love it, so we figured why not be a community shop for the Upper East Side. We're not just a dispensary, we're an art gallery too — we procured art from Paris, Switzerland, a lot of New York artists are featured, and some of the most expensive and exquisite pipe pieces you'll ever see are displayed in my store, some $15,000 to $20,000 pieces, and I think we'll sell maybe three a year.

Bryan Fields: Was the whole process intentional, understanding the demographics and positioning assets around them so people feel like they're walking into a store consistent with their local community?

Markel Bababekov: Absolutely, exactly right. When people walk into my store for the first time, there's going to be a wow on everybody's face. The process to get a product in and out is seamless — if you know what you want, order on the self-ordering station, the bud tender has it ready within two or three minutes, you're out. If you're a new user and don't know what you want, bud tenders will walk you to the vape section or flower section with the menu in hand. While people wait, we have benches so they can enjoy the art on the walls and look at the expensive glass. Two or three times a month we'll have events — this month AJ, the creator of Sour Diesel, is going to be our guest bud tender. We also have a local artist doing a print release for his new work at our location.

Bryan Fields: Let's fast forward — you've gone through a tremendous journey from April to now, right on the edge about to open. Take us through your feelings today, January 2nd, before you open.

Markel Bababekov: You know what, man, I think my smile says it all. Just hearing you say this gives me chills. We're finally about to open through all this. I've never been so overwhelmed in my life. I'm getting maybe 100 emails a day, I have two phones ringing off the hook all day — vendor trainings, because every vendor needs to train my bud tenders, plus I hired a training staff for the POS system and operating procedures. I had to host so many interviews to hire my whole staff, we have a staff of 20 now — managers, assistant managers, bud tenders, inventory — I was getting like 150 resumes a minute. I had to get a merchant for credit card, cashless ATM, debit transfers, ATMs — I've never signed more contracts in my life than in the last 30 days, all the onboarding, missing half my scheduled calls because I'm so busy. It's been the most overwhelming time of my life, and I'm so happy about it, I love every minute of it.

Bryan Fields: What's been your favorite part of the process — going to the farms, trying all the cannabis?

Markel Bababekov: There are two brands I really want to feature. One is AJ Sour Diesel — real Sour Diesel, the strain I grew up with as a kid from Queens, rolling my first blunt to my last blunt, always asking for sour. I smelled it, smoked it, tried it — I think people are really going to appreciate that there's a real Sour Diesel strain from the owner who created the original one back in the '80s. That's huge. And Mike Tyson's gummies — I really want to highlight those, they're incredible. There's also one specific farm that stood out among all the great ones I visited — I don't want to name the others because they were all great too, but this one is called MFNY, Marijuana Farms New York. Their concentrates, vapes, and flower impressed me so much that they're going to have two displays in my store, the only brand to get that. Very high quality for a great price, amazing margins. I think that brand specifically is going to be flying off the shelves.

Bryan Fields: As a New York boy, I'm excited for the Sour Diesel.

Markel Bababekov: You know right away, exactly. And Sour Diesel, man, I know a lot of people haven't had real sour in so long, and this stuff is amazing. I'm very happy to have it in my store.

Bryan Fields: Let's slightly switch gears — dream smoking session, three people, dead or alive.

Markel Bababekov: Biggie, Eminem, and... let me think... George Bush. I want to smoke a joint with George Bush and find out what the hell went on during his administration — probably more than a joint.

Bryan Fields: What is the most expensive lesson you've ever learned?

Markel Bababekov: Actually in this space, for this store, with a contractor. I needed electrical done for the whole store — brand new electrical, we turned one big box into five offices, a basement, so much work. I went to a few companies giving me crazy prices, almost six figures, then met two guys who said, 'You can pay me by the day,' and I said that sounds good. What these guys pulled on me was ridiculous — I lost about $35,000 to $40,000 more on labor because of them. They'd bring a whole crew, look busy but not really busy, and my cameras weren't up yet, I was still traveling back and forth to LA, my brother still had the dry cleaners, so I was going heavy on trust and shouldn't have. I paid seven guys a day, five days a week, for almost two months, way over what it should have cost — about $30,000 more than what I should have paid professionals. That was one of the most painful lessons because on such a tight budget, that $30,000 could have gone to marketing, media, millwork, or payroll, and we just blew it in the air. It shows that trying to save a dollar by taking the cheaper route can cost you a dime.

Bryan Fields: If you could put anything on a billboard, metaphorically speaking, to get a message to billions of people — image, quote, word, what's the first thing that comes to mind?

Markel Bababekov: Legal weed.

Bryan Fields: What question do you wish more people asked you?

Markel Bababekov: I think more people should be open to getting product knowledge. I've been a marijuana connoisseur my whole adult life, started smoking at 14, was smoking almost an eighth a day until the last couple years when I switched to vapes. I thought I knew so much about cannabis, but going into this space, learning about the plants, the extraction process, there's so much more to learn. No matter how many years you've smoked, come inside and ask questions about the products — you might buy something just because the packaging is nice and not like it, so ask questions for product knowledge, and I promise you'll find something you'll love.

Bryan Fields: Prediction time, Markel — what is the number one thing you would do to improve the licensing process so others don't face a similar path?

Markel Bababekov: I'd hire more people at OCM to communicate with license holders. That's been one big problem for me and a lot of other CAURD holders — lack of communication. It's not their fault, they're so busy with the rollout of all these dispensaries, stressed out themselves, but lack of communication was a big issue. There was a lot we needed to know that was very hard to get from them.

Kellan Finney: I think New York maybe caught a hint of perfectionism trying to roll out their market — wanting to do something so perfect that they had a hard time putting out a first draft, when any first draft is going to have errors you fix later. A potential solution could be making licensing more like opening a liquor store in terms of the hoops you jump through, and reallocating resources to enforcement with boots on the ground, which could also help regulate the illicit market.

Markel Bababekov: I agree wholeheartedly with that. The first rollout was for justice-involved applicants, the second rollout for licenses is a lottery. And honestly, not that many people apply for these licenses — if you look at the actual list of CAURD applicants, it's not that many, same with the general license applicants. I told a lot of people about this opportunity and they didn't seem to know about it — lack of marketing on OCM's end. A lot of people just didn't know about this big golden opportunity.

Bryan Fields: I think to expand on your point, the reason people don't act is because they're intimidated to take action. The idea of something is fun, but actually sitting down and overcoming obstacles when you don't know how to do things is hard — no one knows the answer, you have to seek it out, put yourself in uncomfortable situations regularly, and have the ability to show up again tomorrow. I commend you for sticking through it and doubling down when things were tough. I think with your mindset and skill set you'll really benefit the community, and it's exciting to see what the future holds for you here in New York.

Markel Bababekov: Thank you, that means a lot, man, thank you so much.

Bryan Fields: So Markel, for our listeners who want to get in touch, who want to visit your store, where can they find you?

Markel Bababekov: 1412 Lexington Avenue, New York, New York, 10128, Upper East Side, on Lexington between 92nd and 93rd. It's a big, big store, right in the middle of the block, you can't miss us — it says The Herbal Care.

Bryan Fields: We'll link it all up in the show notes. Thanks for taking the time, this was fun.

Markel Bababekov: Thank you.
summary: This episode of The Dime features Markel Bababekov, owner of The Herbal Care, a CAURD-licensed dispensary on Manhattan's Upper East Side, discussing his journey from cannabis processing in Los Angeles to becoming one of New York's first legal cannabis retailers. He details the grueling process of finding a location amid predatory landlord practices and a cannabis-specific rent tax, the emotional rollercoaster of surviving New York's CAURD licensing injunction while continuing an expensive buildout, and his strategy of differentiating his upscale, art-gallery-style store from the illicit shops flooding the city. The conversation offers a candid, ground-level look at the real costs, risks, and regulatory chaos facing first-time social equity dispensary operators in New York's emerging legal cannabis market.
takeaways: Markel Bababekov leveraged his justice-involved status and prior cannabis industry experience to qualify for New York's CAURD (Conditional Adult-Use Retail Dispensary) license.
Landlords routinely added a roughly 25% 'cannabis tax' on rent and offered zero negotiating power to CAURD licensees, unlike standard commercial leasing.

When the CAURD program was hit with a court injunction, OCM could no longer communicate with license holders, forcing Bababekov to continue his buildout blind, based only on regulations and legal counsel.
Making the 'short list' of dispensaries allowed to open during the injunction was a turning point that justified the risk of continuing to invest despite the shutdown.
The state's DASNY-administered social equity fund had loan terms and equity buyout conditions the guest considered predatory, leading him to self-fund the business with his brother instead.

Illicit/unlicensed smoke shops are often identifiable by heavy weed-themed exterior marketing and visible product, while licensed dispensaries like The Herbal Care intentionally keep storefronts discreet per regulation.
Cutting corners on contractors to save money backfired, costing an estimated extra $30,000-$40,000 in labor overruns on electrical work.
A lack of communication and marketing from OCM meant relatively few people even applied for CAURD or general licenses despite it being a major opportunity.

faq.question: What is the CAURD program mentioned in this episode?
faq.answer: CAURD stands for Conditional Adult-Use Retail Dispensary, New York's first licensing round for cannabis retail, prioritized for justice-involved individuals and entrepreneurs with existing qualifying businesses.

faq.question: Why did landlords charge cannabis dispensaries extra rent in New York?
faq.answer: According to the guest, landlords routinely added an informal cannabis-specific premium of around 25% to asking rent once they learned a tenant was a licensed cannabis retailer, with little to no room for negotiation.

faq.question: What was the CAURD injunction and how did it affect license holders?
faq.answer: A court-ordered injunction froze parts of New York's cannabis licensing rollout, cutting off communication between OCM (Office of Cannabis Management) and license holders and leaving many operators, including Markel Bababekov, uncertain whether they'd ever be able to open despite having already signed leases and started buildouts.

faq.question: How can consumers tell a legal dispensary apart from an illicit cannabis shop in New York?
faq.answer: Per the guest, illicit shops tend to display heavy cannabis-leaf branding and visible product through their windows, while licensed dispensaries are required to keep storefronts discreet with blacked-out windows and no visible product from outside.

faq.question: What was DASNY's role in New York's cannabis licensing and why did the guest avoid it?
faq.answer: DASNY (Dormitory Authority of the State of New York) administered a social equity fund meant to provide loans and build-out support to CAURD licensees, but the guest found its loan terms and equity buyout clauses unfavorable and chose to self-fund his dispensary with his brother instead.

faq.question: Why did the guest choose the Upper East Side over a tourist location like Times Square?
faq.answer: After initially pursuing Times Square storefronts for tourist traffic, he pivoted to the Upper East Side, an area he knew well from living there for years, deciding a community-focused, art-gallery-style dispensary fit that neighborhood's demographics better than a tourist destination model.

faq.question: What is one of the most expensive mistakes the guest made during buildout?
faq.answer: He hired day-rate electrical contractors to save money, but they padded hours and appeared busy without efficient work, ultimately costing him an estimated $30,000 to $40,000 more than hiring licensed professionals upfront would have.

faq.question: What does the guest suggest to improve New York's cannabis licensing process going forward?
faq.answer: He recommends OCM hire more staff dedicated to communicating directly with license holders, and better market the licensing opportunity itself, since he found surprisingly few people even applied for CAURD or general licenses.
